Nasdaq slides 1.2% amid renewed pressure on AI stocks
sum: US technology stocks extended their losses on Thursday as Wall Street reacted to the Democrats’ midterm election victories, with investors concerned that increased political scrutiny could slow the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.2% to 25,427.44 at the opening bell, continuing a difficult week for technology shares as investors reassessed the outlook for AI-related investment and regulation.
The broader S&P 500 declined 0.4% to 7,654.89, reflecting weakness among major technology companies that have played an important role in driving US equity market gains.
However, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.5% to 53,595.12, highlighting a divergence between technology stocks and more traditional sectors of the American economy.

Investors appeared to be rotating away from technology shares towards established industrial and other non-technology businesses, amid concerns that Democratic lawmakers could seek greater oversight of AI development and the rapid expansion of data centres.
The election results have brought renewed attention to the electricity consumption, infrastructure requirements and local environmental impact of large-scale AI facilities.

Potential restrictions on new data centre developments could affect expectations for future spending on semiconductors, servers and supporting infrastructure, although the scale and timing of any regulatory changes remain uncertain.

Down 9% in 3 months, could BAE Systems shares be one of the FTSE 100’s best bargains?
sum: BAE Systems' (LSE:BA.) shares are currently (3 November) changing hands for 9% less than they were in the middle of August, and 11% lower than in March, when the stock recorded its 52-week high.
Does this mean the defence contractor's shares are now a bargain?
Savvy investors know that short-term price movements are largely irrelevant. Although it's difficult to ignore monthly fluctuations, it's the long-term trend that matters.

And a look at the graph for BAE Systems shows that its share price has been going in the right direction over the past five years. In fact, since October 2021, it's increased by 275%. This makes it the fourth-best performer on the FTSE 100.

And as the biggest supplier to the Ministry of Defence, I think further growth's likely. On Wednesday (28 October), the UK Chancellor confirmed the government's commitment to meet the NATO target of spending 3% of Gross Domestic Product on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035.
Although no details were provided as to how this was going to be achieved, it stands to reason that BAE Systems will be one of the beneficiaries.

Why? Well, the group's firmly embedded within the UK's military infrastructure — for example, it plays a vital role in supporting the country's nuclear-powered submarines — which means its order book is likely to grow in line with government spending on defence.

items.t: European Stock Markets Today: FTSE MIB, DAX 40, CAC 40 and FTSE 100 Rally as Oil and Bond Yields Ease
sum: Italy’s FTSE MIB led with a 1.29% gain to about 49,187, the DAX 40 rose 0.91% to 25,410.84, the CAC 40 added 0.83% to 7,847.32 and the FTSE 100 climbed 0.72% to 10,767.33. The Euro Stoxx 50 gained 0.79% to 6,116.23.

Three forces drove the session. Oil prices eased as mediators travelled to Tehran and Washington reviewed a possible Iran deal; Moody’s decision late on Friday to keep France’s Aa3 rating unchanged pushed French borrowing costs sharply lower; and defence and technology stocks rebounded after Anthropic’s IPO filing in the United States revived appetite for AI-linked shares. Each section below covers the closing level, the drivers, the leading and lagging stocks and what to watch next.
FTSE 100 Rises 0.72% to 10,767.33 as Computacenter Soars 13% and Defence Stocks Rebound Ahead of the UK Budget

London’s blue-chip index made a solid start to Budget week, lifted by a profit upgrade from Computacenter and a sharp rebound in Rolls-Royce, BAE Systems and Babcock, while Experian and the oil majors weighed.

The FTSE 100 closed at 10,767.33 points on Monday, 26 October 2026, up 76.97 points or 0.72% from Friday’s close of 10,690.36, according to Reuters and Alliance News closing data. The mid-cap FTSE 250 did even better, rising 1.09% to 24,501.25, its biggest one-day gain since 9 October. The AIM All-Share added 0.9% to 753.18.

The gain came despite a weak session in Asia and recovered part of the ground the index lost last week, when it had closed at 10,752.88 on Wednesday before slipping as oil hit a five-month high. The FTSE 100 remains about 2% below its July record near 10,991.
“The FTSE 100 made a solid start to Budget week as oil prices eased back and despite weak trading across Asia,” said Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell.

Third 6th-Gen Fighter Program Bubbles in Europe as Germany Explores Spain-Sweden Deal
sum: As Germany seeks a new partner to develop its next-generation fighter after the collapse of FCAS, it now faces two choices: join the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP) or forge a new partnership with Sweden and Spain.
If the proposal materializes, Europe could have three sixth-generation fighter programs: GCAP and the French initiative.

In June 2026, the Friedrich Merz administration pulled the plug on the FCAS (Future Combat Air System) that it was pursuing with France and Spain, over irreconcilable differences between industry partners Airbus (representing Germany and Spain) and France’s Dassault Aviation.
Berlin has been seeking a partnership to develop a sixth-generation aircraft ever since.

Earlier this month, reports indicated it held “exploratory talks” about joining the GCAP led by the UK, Japan, and Italy, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham officially raised Germany’s involvement in GCAP.
However, Airbus had also earlier hinted it could potentially partner with Swedish defense manufacturer Saab to develop its sixth-generation fighter.
German defense officials have reportedly encouraged Berlin to seek a new fighter-aircraft collaboration with Sweden and Spain rather than join an existing deal involving the United Kingdom.

sum: BAE Systems (LSE: BA) shares' 18% drop from their 18 March £23.59 one-year high suggests many investors believe the global security environment is improving. I completely disagree.
The war in Ukraine is ongoing, as is that between the US and Iran, and Iran and Israel. Indeed, the Tehran-backed Houthis have widened the war with attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Even if these conflicts stopped tomorrow, a massive increase in NATO's long-term defence spending has already been agreed. The organisation pledged 5% of GDP to go on defence by 2035. That means a rise of around 64% from today. And as Europe's largest defence firm and the world's sixth-largest, BAE is perfectly positioned to benefit from that.
The 20 main analysts covering BAE have a 12-month price target of £23.23. That represents a 20.4% rise from the £19.29 level at the time of writing.

Bullish sentiment was boosted following BAE's strong H1 2026 results released on 30 July. Management raised full-year guidance across the board for all key measures. For example, underlying earnings before interest and taxes growth was increased from 9%-11% to 10%-12%. It is growth in earnings that is the key driver of share price gains for any stock.
Sales growth guidance jumped from 7%-9% to 8%-10%, and the free cash flow forecast soared 54% to £2bn.

Analysts' confidence in the defence giant achieving these new numbers stems from the strong multi-decade order book. In fact, the H1 numbers saw new orders climb 24% year on year to £16.4bn, with an £84bn order backlog. These figures — and the several massive multi-year deals included within them — provide exceptional earnings visibility for the company.

Down 20%, could BAE Systems shares have more potential than Rolls-Royce?
sum: After a powerful multi-year rally, BAE Systems' (LSE: BA.) shares have experienced a pullback. Currently, they're trading near £19 – around 20% below their all-time highs.
Could they offer more potential than shares in industrial rival Rolls-Royce (LSE: RR.) after this dip? Let's discuss.

BAE Systems' shares are certainly a lot cheaper than Rolls-Royce shares at the moment. Looking at earnings forecasts for 2026, they're currently trading on a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 23.
Rolls-Royce shares are sporting a P/E ratio of 34. So they're almost 50% more expensive.

Of course, a P/E ratio in isolation is pretty useless. To get value out of this ratio, we need to look at lots of other factors like revenue and earnings growth, long-term growth potential, and financial strength.
So let's compare the two companies. Could Rolls-Royce's higher valuation actually be worth it?
This year and next, BAE Systems is expected to generate revenue growth of 18% and 9%. Earnings per share are expected to rise 12% and 14%.

Defense stocks fall after NATO Summit 🚩 Rheinmetall drops 4%, KNDS suspends IPO
sum: - Rheinmetall is down nearly 4% despite maintaining a highly favorable long-term outlook for European defense spending.
- Investors are increasingly focusing on contract execution and operational performance rather than additional political commitments to higher defense budgets.
- KNDS' suspended IPO suggests that institutional investors have become significantly more cautious toward the European defense sector.
- Weaker sentiment is also evident across other major European defense stocks, including BAE Systems, Dassault Aviation, Leonardo, Saab, and Kongsberg Gruppen

Shares of Rheinmetall (RHM.DE) are down nearly 4% following the NATO summit in Ankara, while the broader European defense sector is also trading under pressure despite the alliance reaffirming its commitment to strengthening military capabilities. The move may signal that investors are shifting away from buying the defense narrative and are beginning to evaluate companies based on execution and fundamentals.

At first glance, the market reaction appears counterintuitive. NATO has effectively confirmed the long-term trend of rising defense spending, while Europe's largest defense contractors continue to enjoy record order backlogs. In theory, Rheinmetall shares should be moving higher.

The problem is that markets price the future, not the present. Much of the positive news has already been reflected in share prices following the extraordinary rally of the past two years. Once valuations become elevated, investors begin asking different questions: How quickly can companies execute their contracts? Can they maintain margins? Will political commitments ultimately translate into sustainable earnings and free cash flow?

Is BAE Systems Expanding Its Presence in the Naval MRO Market?
sum: BAE Systems BAESY continues to strengthen its position in the global naval maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO) market through its broad portfolio of ship repair, modernization and sustainment services for military vessels. The company plays an important role in supporting the operational readiness of the U.S. Navy and allied naval forces by providing maintenance, upgrades and lifecycle support for a wide range of naval platforms.

BAE Systems operates one of the largest naval ship repair businesses in the United States, providing maintenance, overhaul, modernization and technical support for amphibious assault ships, destroyers, cruisers and other surface combatants. Its capabilities help extend the service life of naval vessels, improve mission readiness and ensure fleet remain operational in increasingly demanding environments.

Growing geopolitical tensions, rising global defense spending and increasing investments in naval fleet modernization are driving demand for maintenance, repair and overhaul services worldwide. As navies look to extend the operational life of existing vessels while maintaining combat readiness, demand for advanced sustainment and modernization solutions is expected to remain strong.

BAE Systems is well-positioned to benefit from these long-term industry trends through its extensive experience in naval ship repair and modernization, supported by long-standing relationships with the U.S. Navy and allied defense customers. Its strong portfolio of maintenance and sustainment capabilities should enable the company to capitalize on the growing demand for naval MRO services.
Other aerospace and defense companies strengthening their presence in the naval maintenance, repair and overhaul market are discussed below:

General Dynamics GD: Through its Marine Systems business, General Dynamics provides lifecycle support, modernization, engineering and sustainment services for the U.S. Navy's submarine and surface ship fleet, alongside its shipbuilding operations.

Huntington Ingalls Industries HII: Through its Newport News Shipbuilding and Ingalls Shipbuilding divisions, HII provides maintenance, modernization, refueling and overhaul services for aircraft carriers, submarines and other naval vessels, supporting long-term fleet readiness.

BAE Systems Shares Surge as UK’s £15bn Defence Boost Fuels Rally
sum: BAE Systems (LON: BA.) shares surged more than 6% on Thursday, hitting a high of 2,006p before settling around 1,993p as the defence giant extended a powerful two-day rally sparked by the UK government’s long-delayed Defence Investment Plan.

The move has now added well over £3 billion to BAE’s market value since Tuesday’s close, on volume of more than 4 million shares, as investors piled into the stock following confirmation of major new government spending commitments squarely aligned with BAE’s core operations.

Published Tuesday after weeks of delay — a delay that had already cost one Defence Secretary his job — the plan confirms £15 billion in additional funding over four years, taking total planned defence spending to around £300 billion and pushing outlays to 2.7% of GDP by 2029.

Crucially, the money flows directly into BAE’s businesses: £8.6 billion for the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP), £63 billion for nuclear deterrent and submarine work, £11 billion for munitions, and £5 billion for drones and autonomous naval systems — covering combat-air, naval, weapons and autonomy divisions alike.
CEO Charles Woodburn told Reuters the funding is “vital to sustaining the specialist skills” underpinning the UK’s defence industrial base.

The rally has been reinforced by bullish broker commentary and appears to have gathered further momentum through Thursday’s session as investors and defence-sector funds continued buying. The gain now vastly outstrips the firepower of BAE’s own £500 million buyback programme launched last month.
Some caution remains: a £4.7 billion funding shortfall in the UK is still unresolved, with defence chiefs having sought £28 billion rather than £15 billion. BAE reports half-year results on July 30.

sum: Now around 1,885p each, BAE Systems‘ (LSE:BA.) shares have performed splendidly for me since I bought them at 819p in November 2022. I also added twice on weakness in 2024.

However, since peaking at 2,360p in March, BAE’s slumped 20%. And the defence stock’s now gone sideways over the past 12 months, noticeably lagging the FTSE 100‘s 19% return. That’s quite disappointing.
The question I’m asking myself now is, should I recycle my gains into a different stock?

On one level, I’m not worried about BAE stock specifically as it has been caught up in a wider defence sector sell-off. In fact, it’s fared relatively well compared to others like Babcock International (down 33% since January) and Rheinmetall (down 45% since January).

And while the wars in Ukraine and Iran are hopefully going to end sooner rather than later, they won’t just be forgotten about. NATO allies and Gulf states are still committed to beefing up defence capabilities for any future conflicts.
But will Europe actually find the money to re-arm properly? After all, Germany just abandoned its planned six-ship F126 frigate programme.

Meanwhile, we’ve seen recently how the UK government has struggled to stump up what many military experts say is needed to defend the realm. Remember, Western European economies are stagnant and heavily indebted.
